questions.question: A planet's average temperature holds steady only while it sends as much energy out to space as it absorbs from sunlight. Norman Loeb, a NASA scientist, and his colleagues compared satellite measurements of both flows and reported in 2021 that Earth now absorbs more than it sends out, a gap that roughly doubled from 2005 to 2019. Where has most of the extra energy gone?
choices: Into the oceans
Into the air
Into the land
Into melting ice
questions.context: By the reckoning of Karina von Schuckmann and her colleagues in 2023, about 89 percent of the heat Earth has gained since 1971 is in the oceans, about 6 percent in the land and about 4 percent has gone into melting ice, while only about 1 percent has warmed the air. Loeb's team checked the satellites against floats that measure how fast the oceans warm. While the imbalance lasts, Earth keeps gaining heat.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade Earth science teaches climate as a balance of energy in and energy out, and where the extra energy is stored.

questions.question: Milutin Milankovic, a Serbian engineer, spent nearly three decades working out, long before computers, how three slow cycles change the sunlight reaching Earth: the tilt of its axis, the stretch of its orbit and the wobble of its axis. He traced the sunlight at 65 degrees north, where the great ice sheets of the ice ages grew. By his reasoning, what lets such an ice sheet grow?
questions.answer: Summers too cool to melt the winter's snow
choices: Summers too cool to melt the winter's snow
Winters cold enough to pile up heavier snow
Winters that come when Earth is farthest from the Sun
Years in which the total sunlight falls sharply
questions.context: Snow that outlasts a cool summer piles up year after year into an ice sheet; Milankovic took the cool-summer idea from the climate scientist Wladimir Köppen. Heavier winter snow does little if the summer melts it all away, a hemisphere whose winter falls when Earth is farthest from the Sun has its summer at the nearest point and so a warmer one, and the cycles hardly change the sunlight the whole Earth gets in a year (the stretch of the orbit by about 0.2 percent) but shift it between seasons and places. His theory was largely ignored for about fifty years, and he died in 1958, before the deep-sea test of it.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade Earth science names changes in Earth's orbit and tilt among the natural causes of climate change, with the ice ages as the example.

questions.question: James Hays, John Imbrie and Nicholas Shackleton read 450,000 years of climate in mud cored from the deep sea floor between Africa, Australia and Antarctica. They were testing Milutin Milankovic's idea that three slow cycles in Earth's orbit and tilt, each tens of thousands of years long, bring on the ice ages. What did they report in 1976?
questions.answer: Climate swings that kept time with all three cycles
choices: Climate swings that kept time with all three cycles
Climate swings that kept time with the tilt alone
Climate swings that missed the longest of the three cycles
Climate swings that kept no steady time at all
questions.context: Oxygen in the shells of tiny sea creatures tracks how much ice stood on land, and the kinds of plankton track the sea's warmth; both swung with periods of about 23,000, 42,000 and 100,000 years, the beats of the wobble, the tilt and the stretching orbit. Milankovic had expected the tilt to matter most, yet the 100,000-year beat was the strongest though it changes the yearly sunlight least, and why is still argued. The orbit sets the pace, and feedbacks such as spreading ice and falling carbon dioxide make the small push large.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn how a prediction is tested against an independent record, and the deep-sea cores of 1976 are the classic test of the orbital theory of the ice ages.

questions.question: Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted in June 1991, and its haze spread around the world high in the air. James Hansen's team at NASA ran the haze through a climate model and published a forecast early in 1992: the world would cool by about half a degree Celsius for a year or two, then warm again later in the decade. What did the world's thermometers show?
questions.answer: A cooling of about the size the model forecast
choices: A cooling of about the size the model forecast
A cooling about twice the size the model forecast
A cooling that lasted decades, far past the forecast
No cooling at all, though the model forecast one
questions.context: Global temperatures fell by about half a degree Celsius, and the journal Science reported early in 1993 that the forecast had been on target, though a later account notes that the model cooled the world a little too much. The cooling lasted one to three years. A forecast published before the event is a fair test of a model, because the answer cannot have been fitted to it afterwards.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science teaches that volcanic eruptions can cool the climate and that a model earns trust by predicting a result before it is seen.

questions.question: Arctic sea ice shrinks every summer and grows back every winter. In a warm summer it shrinks further than usual and leaves wide stretches of open sea, and climate scientists say such a loss tends to speed itself up before the summer ends. What makes it do so?
questions.answer: The dark water absorbs sunlight the ice would reflect
choices: The dark water absorbs sunlight the ice would reflect
The meltwater leaves the sea saltier, so it freezes less easily
The melting ice gives off heat that warms the sea around it
The sea water needs less heat than ice to warm up
questions.context: Snow-covered ice reflects about 80 to 90 percent of the sunlight that strikes it and open sea less than a tenth, so each patch of ice lost lets in more heat and melts more ice. Melting in fact soaks up heat, sea ice is far less salty than sea water, and water needs about twice as much heat as ice to warm. A feedback like this one, or the extra water vapour that warmer air holds, strengthens a change that something else began, and other effects push back: after the record low of 2012, the 2013 summer ice was far larger.
questions.grade_note: The ninth-grade curriculum names this feedback directly: melting ice uncovers darker ground and sea that absorb more sunlight.

questions.question: Rock about 50 million years old on Ellesmere Island, in the Canadian Arctic, holds fossil alligators, giant tortoises and the wood and leaves of dawn redwood trees, where only tundra plants grow today. Oxygen in the animals' bones and teeth suggests that winters there rarely, if ever, froze. What best explains so warm an Arctic in that age, the Eocene?
questions.answer: Earth as a whole was far warmer than it is now
choices: Earth as a whole was far warmer than it is now
The island lay near the equator and drifted north
Earth's axis stood nearly upright, with no seasons
The Sun shone far more brightly than it does now
questions.context: The early Eocene was roughly 12 degrees Celsius warmer than before industry, with little or no ice anywhere and carbon dioxide estimated at about 700 to 1,600 parts per million, against about 430 today. Rock magnetism puts the island at about 75 to 80 degrees north then, close to where it lies now; the Moon keeps Earth's tilt between about 22 and 24.5 degrees; and the Sun, which brightens by about 1 percent every 110 million years, was a little dimmer. Antarctica's great ice sheet began to grow only about 34 million years ago, as the world cooled.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade Earth science uses the fossil record to show that climate has changed over Earth's history, and the warm Eocene Arctic is the standard example.

questions.question: The Thames froze across at London in 24 winters between 1400 and 1831, and in the hardest frosts Londoners held fairs on the ice, the last in 1814. Those centuries fell in the Little Ice Age, a cool era that ended around 1850. Raphael Neukom's team compared records of past climate kept in tree rings, corals, ice cores and lake mud from around the world, and reported the result in 2019. What did the team find about when the cold came?
questions.answer: Different regions were coldest in different centuries
choices: Different regions were coldest in different centuries
Every region was coldest in the same few decades
Only Europe cooled, while the rest of the world did not
The cold spread steadily from the poles to the equator
questions.context: Neukom's team found the coldest stretch of the last thousand years in the 1400s in the central and eastern Pacific, in the 1600s in northwestern Europe and southeastern North America, and in the mid-1800s across most other regions; of the Little Ice Age, Neukom said 'it was generally colder across the whole world, but not everywhere at the same time', though Michael Evans, a climate scientist at the University of Maryland, cautioned that such findings grow less certain the further back they reach. A frozen river is not a plain thermometer either: the old London Bridge's nineteen narrow arches slowed the Thames and let ice dam it, and its wide-arched replacement of 1831 and the Victorian embankments then quickened the flow.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn how scientists read past climate from natural records such as tree rings and ice cores, and to ask whether one place's record speaks for the whole world.

questions.question: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) drew on more than 14,000 studies for its long 2021 report, which opens with a short Summary for Policymakers. It found the world about 1.1 degrees Celsius warmer than in the late 1800s, called it unequivocal that people had warmed it, and judged that doubling the air's carbon dioxide would likely warm it 2.5 to 4 degrees. Steven Koonin, a physicist and a former Under Secretary for Science at the US Energy Department, published Unsettled that year. What did he argue?
questions.answer: That the summary and the press overstate the certainty
choices: That the summary and the press overstate the certainty
That the full report hides the doubts its summary admits
That the world has not warmed since the late 1800s
That people's gases have had no part in the warming
questions.context: Earth warmed by about 1.1 degrees Celsius from the late 1800s to the 2010s and by about 1.3 to 1.4 degrees by 2024, and Koonin accepts both the warming and a human part in it, a push he has called 'physically small in relation to the climate system as a whole'; in 2014 he wrote that an official 'reading only the IPCC's "Summary for Policy Makers" would gain little sense' of the models' shortcomings, and he built Unsettled from the report's technical chapters. Critics such as the economist Gary Yohe, writing in Scientific American, and the climate scientist Benjamin Santer answered that scientists discuss these uncertainties openly, and others noted that he leaned on IPCC reports of 2013 and 2014 that newer ones had overtaken. Climate scientists name clouds as the main reason the range for doubled carbon dioxide is still so wide.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science asks students to tell a measured finding from a judgement about its certainty, and to name who makes each claim on a contested question.

questions.question: Al Gore, a former Vice President of the United States, told a meeting beside the United Nations climate talks in Copenhagen in December 2009 that models suggested to Wieslaw Maslowski, a sea-ice scientist, 'a 75 per cent chance' that 'the entire north polar ice cap' could be 'completely ice-free' in summer within five to seven years. Maslowski said he could not see how that figure had been arrived at. What did satellites show over the next seven summers?
questions.answer: Ice every summer, below its 1979 to 2000 average
choices: Ice every summer, below its 1979 to 2000 average
Ice every summer, near its 1979 to 2000 average
Ice every summer, above its 1979 to 2000 average
No ice at all in at least one summer
questions.context: Ice-free means less than 1 million square kilometres of sea ice; the smallest September cover on record, in 2012, was about 3.4 million, about half the average of 1979 to 2000, and ice has remained every summer since. The record holds both halves: the summer ice is shrinking by about 12 percent a decade, and the dated forecast failed. Maslowski had projected a nearly ice-free summer, possibly as early as 2013, and said he had been explicit that he meant nearly, not completely; Gore's office said the 75 percent was a ballpark figure Maslowski had used in a conversation years before.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn that a prediction with a date can be checked against later measurements, and to report both what was forecast and what was then observed.

questions.question: Zaichun Zhu's team reported in 2016 that satellites had watched a quarter to half of Earth's vegetated land turn significantly greener since the early 1980s, and computer models credited most of it to the extra carbon dioxide in the air. Chi Chen's team then reported in 2019 that China and India, with only 9 percent of the world's vegetated land, gave a third of the new green leaf from 2000 to 2017. What did Chen's team credit for that share?
choices: Tree planting and intensive farming
Extra carbon dioxide in the air
Warmer and wetter weather
Wild forests spreading back on their own
questions.context: The new leaf came mainly from China's tree-planting programmes and from intensive farming in both countries. The finding does not rule out carbon dioxide feeding plant growth, which the models of 2016 credited with about 70 percent of the greening worldwide; Zhu's co-authors noted that those shares come from models and that the boost may fade as plants adjust. Both studies measured the change from orbit, and by 2017 the world carried about 5 percent more green leaf than in the early 2000s.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn that satellites monitor Earth's systems and that one trend can have several causes, each named by the study that found it.
